originalTitle: Elle’s twins played with asbestos-contaminated coloured sand for a year. Why wasn’t she warned of its danger?
summary: A New Zealand couple has fought to uncover why customers were originally told the children’s product, on sale in Australia, was ‘low risk’
content: When Elle Chrisp learned her twins were playing with coloured sand from Kmart that could be contaminated with asbestos, she thought she had the problem sorted. “When the recall happened I read the notice, saw the words ‘low risk’, and followed the instructions to double-bag the sand so it was ready to be chucked out,” Chrisp tells the Guardian from her home in Christchurch, New Zealand. “I was like, ‘This is OK, this isn’t scary’, we’ll just do as it says, bag it up, and throw it out.’” Eight months later, Chrisp and her husband, Dave Dingwall, were shocked to learn that when they and thousands of other consumers were told the products were low risk unless mechanically processed, regulators hadn’t tested it. In fact, when scientists tested the sand, simulating children’s play, most of them did release toxic airborne asbestos fibres. But by this stage, the safety messaging had already spread widely. To discover the truth, the parents were forced to undertake their own exhaustive research, doggedly pushing for answers after contacting officials and being met with closed doors. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Eventually, they launched a compensation claim against Kmart in New Zealand’s disputes tribunal, with a decision expected to be handed down next week. ‘Low risk’ Last November, Educational Colours sand products sold at 80 different retailers, including major Australian chain Officeworks, were recalled after samples were found to contain asbestos. Next came the recall of a range of sand products sold at Kmart, including one that Chrisp and Dingwall’s young twins had been playing with for about a year. The parents, both 37, were mollified by Kmart’s recall notice, which assured them the products were low risk and fibres were unlikely to be released into the air unless the sand was processed by mechanical means such as crushing or pulverising. Chrisp and Dingwall would later discover that Kmart had copied Educational Colours’ safety assurances, despite not relating to any of its products, which had been imported by a different supplier, and without any evidence of its own. They made the discovery by combing through a trove of documents released under freedom of information laws, which included emails between Kmart and NZ government officials, and the minutes from a meeting between the parties in December 2025. At that meeting, WorkSafe NZ told senior Kmart representatives it had a “high level of confidence” that the products contained dangerous asbestos fibres that could become airborne. Nevertheless, the Kmart representatives told the meeting there had been “customer confusion and hysteria” about the sand. Kmart did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment. Alarm bells started ringing for Chrisp when she read in a newspaper that a Kmart store had been shut and professionally decontaminated by a licensed asbestos removalist after an open tub of sand was found in the staff room. “I thought, wait: that same sand had been through my home and my children’s hands, yet our notice told parents to put it in the bin,” Chrisp says. “If it warranted closing a store for Kmart, why were we told ‘low risk’? That contradiction is what sent Dave and me looking.” A former lawyer, Chrisp became determined to find out why parents in Australia and New Zealand were being told the products were “low risk”. The source of the misinformation While Chrisp and Dingwall watched with dismay as the retailer’s safety claim become the de facto position of the Australian and New Zealand governments, they began asking officials where the “low risk” and “crushing or pulverising” language came from. “No agency could point to any evidence behind it,” Chrisp says. On 28 May this year, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) told Chrisp and Dingwall – in an email seen by the Guardian – it had been provided the information “in confidence” and did not “have consent to release” it. The ACCC suggested the couple contact suppliers undertaking the recalls directly to ask for it. But they felt they were not taken seriously. “When we were asking the questions, it was like we were being difficult,” Chrisp says. “But we were actually just wanting to say, ‘OK, cool, you guys know why this is the case. Can we also know?’ And that part seemed to be very difficult to share with us.” It took eight months of continued chasing, and a complaint to the ombudsman, before the New Zealand government finally released the report that showed the source of the now-contested safety advice: a risk assessment that Educational Colours itself commissioned, which did not involve any additional testing or even a visual inspection of the contaminated products, and was never made public. By this stage, the inaccurate safety advice was being used by schools. The couple’s shock after learning about its origin was compounded when the sand was finally tested and the results published. The Auckland University of Technology (AUT) tests, published last month, found 90% of craft sand samples did release asbestos into the air when played with, contradicting the previous advice. The AUT study, which is yet to be peer reviewed, determined the sand products “can create a real risk from fibres in the air”, although “the magnitude of this risk has yet to be determined by further research”. “Nevertheless, no amount of risk of asbestos exposure through toys is acceptable so the most practical way to eliminate this risk would be to avoid the use of artificial sand products in toys or similar consumer products,” the report says. Dingwall says artificial sand products that are “very, very similar or perhaps identical” to those that were recalled are still for sale in Australia, and they should be banned until appropriate controls are put in place. “Leaving people in the dark is not the same as protecting them,” says Chrisp. “There’s just an inherent risk with this stuff because of the way it’s produced,” Dingwall adds. “It isn’t beach san
chineseTitle: 艾丽的双胞胎在被石棉污染的彩色沙子里玩了一年。为什么没有警告她其危险？
chineseSummary: 一对新西兰夫妇一直在努力寻找消费者最初被告知在澳大利亚销售的儿童产品“低风险”的原因
chineseContent: 当艾丽·克里斯普得知她的双胞胎正在玩凯马特的彩色沙子而沙子可能被石棉污染时，她认为问题已经解决了。克里斯普在新西兰基督城的家中告诉《卫报》：“召回发生时，我读了通知，看到‘低风险’字样，然后按照说明将沙子装进双层袋子，以便准备好扔掉。” “我当时想，‘这没关系，这并不可怕’，我们就按照它说的做，把它包起来，然后扔掉。”八个月后，克里斯普和她的丈夫戴夫·丁沃尔震惊地发现，当他们和数千名其他消费者被告知这些产品除非经过机械加工否则风险较低时，监管机构却没有对其进行测试。事实上，当科学家模拟儿童玩耍对沙子进行测试时，大多数沙子确实释放了有毒的石棉纤维。但到了这个阶段，安全信息已经广泛传播。为了查明真相，家长们被迫进行详尽的调查，在联系官员并进行闭门会面后，顽强地寻求答案。最终，他们向新西兰争议法庭对凯马特提出了赔偿要求，预计下周将做出裁决。 “低风险” 去年 11 月，在 80 家不同零售商（包括澳大利亚大型连锁店 Officeworks）销售的 Educational Colors 沙子产品在样品被发现含有石棉后被召回。接下来是凯马特出售的一系列沙子产品的召回，其中包括克里斯普和丁沃尔的小双胞胎已经玩了大约一年的沙子产品。凯马特的召回通知安抚了这对 37 岁的父母，该通知向他们保证了这些产品的风险较低，并且纤维不太可能释放到食品中。
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
